title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with \(\mathrm{P}=\{x\in R^{d}:Mx\le b\}\) bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within \(p(\mathrm{L}+S)\) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
definitions: The input specifies integers \(m,d\ge 1, M\in Q^{m\times d}\), and \(b\in Q^{m}\). Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: \(v\in \mathrm{P}\) such that \(v=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in \mathrm{P}\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

why: Determine whether an implicit linear description can always be converted into its exact extremal-point representation with polynomial output overhead.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A canonical open problem of enumeration complexity connecting polyhedral computation and optimization. The bounded versus unbounded distinction and long-running algorithmic work give it a separate scientific role from counting or approximate optimization.

progress.text: The revised Reimers–Stougie paper gives total-polynomial enumeration for bounded branch-width while retaining the general bounded-polytope question.
The arrangement-enumeration preprint gives output-sensitive bounds for the vertices of the entire hyperplane arrangement, a different output.

status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The cited bounded-polytope question remains unresolved in the inspected sources. Later searches, including the arrangement-enumeration result, found no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive proof of openness.
review_note: Preserves the approved bounded rational H-to-vertex enumeration target. Explicit output encoding prevents artificial padding from weakening the total-time requirement. Both emptiness and lower-dimensional instances are included.

statement_review.reason: The target and computational model are explicitly specified. This is an editorial review, not a formal verification of the statement or cited proofs.
